summary.text: The Declaration of Independence is the founding document of the United States, adopted unanimously on July 4, 1776 by the Second Continental Congress.
It explains why the Thirteen Colonies regarded themselves as independent states no longer under British rule, citing 27 grievances against the king.
Its famous second sentence says all men are created equal, and the document is among the most influential in history.

facts.value: Thomas Jefferson, who wrote the original draft

items.prompt: A five-member committee had to produce the Declaration. John Adams, a leading supporter of independence, persuaded it to give the first draft to whom?

options.label: Benjamin Franklin
Roger Sherman
Robert R. Livingston
Thomas Jefferson

items.explain: Adams persuaded the Committee of Five to charge Jefferson with writing the original draft, which Congress then edited.

items.prompt: Why was signing the Declaration a dangerous act for the delegates?

options.label: They had promised their own towns they would never sign it
They knew it was high treason against the Crown, punishable by torture and death
It broke the boycott of British goods they had organized
It made them personally owe the debts of the colonial governments

items.explain: The delegates knew that ratifying and signing the document was an act of high treason, which could be punished by torture and death.

items.prompt: Parliament in London taxed colonists who elected no one to it. What did the colonists argue?

options.label: That Parliament had no right to tax them because they were not directly represented in it
That Parliament could tax them only if the colonial courts agreed
That Parliament was free to tax them as long as the king was silent
That Parliament could tax them only on goods they sold overseas

items.explain: Colonists were not directly represented in Parliament, and they argued it had no right to levy taxes upon them.

items.prompt: The British view was that Parliament was supreme throughout the empire. What idea had developed in the colonies instead?

options.label: That each colonial assembly should hold supreme authority over Parliament
That the king alone should decide which rights people may hold
That the British Constitution recognized fundamental rights no government could violate
That the British Constitution applied only to people living in England

items.explain: Colonists came to believe the British Constitution recognized certain fundamental rights that no government, Parliament included, could violate.

items.prompt: What did the Lee Resolution, passed shortly before the Declaration, resolve?

options.label: That Congress should petition the king to repeal the Intolerable Acts
That the British no longer had governing authority over the Thirteen Colonies
That the colonies should boycott British goods until the acts ended
That a committee should be named to write the colonies' charter

items.explain: The Lee Resolution resolved that the British no longer had governing authority over the colonies, and the Declaration then justified that step.

items.prompt: In 1863 Abraham Lincoln built a famous speech around the Declaration. How did he view it?

options.label: As a binding contract that still tied the states to Britain
As a short-term wartime order that the Constitution cancelled
As a list of military victories the nation had to repeat
As a moral standard for the nation, through which the Constitution should be read

items.explain: Lincoln saw the Declaration as the moral standard the United States should strive for and a statement of principles for interpreting the Constitution.

paragraphs.heading: The founding document
paragraphs.text: The Declaration of Independence is the document that founded the United States. It sets out why the Thirteen Colonies saw themselves as independent, sovereign states and no longer under British rule. It gave political, moral and legal reasons for breaking away from the Kingdom of Great Britain. Over time it has become one of the most widely printed, shared and influential documents ever written.

paragraphs.heading: A quarrel over Parliament's power
paragraphs.text: Relations between the colonies and Britain had been getting worse since 1763. Parliament passed measures such as the Stamp Act and the Townshend Acts to raise money from the colonies, which had no direct representatives in Parliament. Colonists argued that Parliament had no right to tax them. The British view held that Parliament was supreme everywhere in the empire, while in the colonies the idea grew that some basic rights could not be broken by any government, Parliament included.

paragraphs.heading: From protest to war
paragraphs.text: In 1774 Parliament passed the Coercive Acts, which the colonists called the Intolerable Acts, to punish them for the Gaspee Affair and the Boston Tea Party. That September the First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia, organized a boycott of British goods and asked the king to repeal the acts. King George and his prime minister, Lord North, were set on enforcing Parliament's supremacy, so these steps failed. By the time independence was declared, the two sides had already been at war for more than a year.

paragraphs.heading: Writing it
paragraphs.text: On June 11, 1776, Congress named the Committee of Five to draft the document: John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, Robert R. Livingston and Roger Sherman. Adams, a strong supporter of independence, persuaded the others to give Jefferson the job of writing the first draft. Jefferson wrote most of it between June 11 and June 28, and Congress then edited his text. It listed 27 grievances against the king and claimed natural and legal rights, among them a right of revolution.

paragraphs.heading: Adoption and danger
paragraphs.text: Two days before adopting it, Congress passed the Lee Resolution, which declared that Britain no longer had authority to govern the colonies. On July 4, 1776, the Second Continental Congress adopted the Declaration unanimously at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia, a building later renamed Independence Hall. The delegates knew that signing it counted as high treason against the Crown, a crime punished by torture and death. These delegates came to be called the Founding Fathers.

paragraphs.heading: Spreading the word
paragraphs.text: The Pennsylvania Evening Post printed the Declaration on July 6. On July 8 at noon, it was read aloud at the same moment in Trenton, Easton and Philadelphia. Printed copies called the Dunlap broadside were handed out widely, and two originals survive at the Library of Congress. The signed copy, hand written by Timothy Matlack and signed mostly on August 2, 1776, is displayed at the National Archives and is usually treated as the official version.

paragraphs.heading: A lasting influence
paragraphs.text: Its second sentence holds that all men are created equal and have unalienable rights, among them life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. That line is counted among the most significant in world history. Abraham Lincoln saw the Declaration as the moral standard the country should aim for, and in 1863 he placed it at the heart of his Gettysburg Address. It has come to stand as a powerful statement on human rights around the world.
